transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, could you tell me what's brought you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Um, well, what finally made me come in is that I just keep forgetting basic adult things, you know? Like paying bills, or returning emails for job interviews... which reminds me, I actually had this one interview last month at this really cool tech startup, and they had this amazing office with, like, a ping-pong table and free snacks, and I was so excited about it. But then I completely forgot to reply to their second email, and by the time I remembered, they had already hired someone else. And it's not just that, I'm missing appointments and forgetting to run errands, and it's just... it's starting to cost me real opportunities, and I don't know what's wrong with me.
Have you struggled with this kind of forgetfulness and disorganization since you were a kid, or is this something that's really only become a problem more recently?

Oh, no, it's definitely been forever. Like, even back in elementary school, my report cards always said the exact same thing. The teachers would write that I was really bright, which was nice, I guess, but they always complained that I constantly lost my worksheets and rushed through all the directions. And I talked out of turn a lot. I just couldn't help it. 

But the disorganization was definitely the worst part. I had a desk that was so incredibly messy I literally could never find my assignments when it was time to turn them in. Actually, one time in third grade, I was digging around in there for a spelling packet and I found a half-eaten sandwich from like, two months prior. It was in a Ziploc bag, thankfully, but my mom had packed me bologna, which I absolutely hate. I don't even know why she bought bologna, I think it was just on sale at Costco? We used to go to Costco every Sunday and I'd always get those giant churros at the food court... they don't even sell the churros anymore, which is an actual tragedy. 

But um... wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, yeah. So I guess the short answer is yes, I've been like this since I was a little kid.
These days, do you often feel restless, fidgety, or like you need to be constantly moving or doing something, or find it hard to sit still for long periods?

Yeah, constantly. It's actually exhausting. Like, if I have to sit through an interview, or a meeting, or even just watch a movie, I get this intense pressure inside my body. It's like I physically need to get up, or shift around, or at least do something with my hands, otherwise I feel like I'm going to literally crawl out of my skin. 

Actually, speaking of movies, I went to see that new superhero one last week with my friend Sarah. Have you seen it? The special effects were wild, but the theater seats were those really nice leather recliners, which you'd think would be great, right? But they made this horrible squeaking noise every single time I moved. And I move a lot. Sarah kept giving me this look, you know, the side-eye, because I was basically doing gymnastics in my chair trying to get comfortable. We've been friends since middle school—we met in band camp, actually. I played the flute, but I was terrible at it because I could never sit still during practice. The band director, Mr. Davis, used to make me run laps around the football field... wait, sorry. Yes, I feel restless all the time. It's really hard to just sit.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes a longstanding (since elementary school) pattern of both inattentive and hyperactive-impulsive symptoms that persist into adulthood and cause functional impairment. Inattentive symptoms include chronic disorganization, losing important materials, forgetting appointments/bills/emails, distractibility, and tangential thinking (evident throughout the interview with frequent unrelated digressions). Hyperactive-impulsive symptoms include pervasive restlessness, inability to sit still, subjective need to move constantly, and a childhood history of interrupting/talking out of turn. Symptoms began before age 12, are present across multiple settings (school, work, social situations), and have caused clear functional consequences (lost job opportunity, missed appointments). This combined presentation of both symptom domains supports ADHD, combined presentation (F90.0), rather than a purely inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive subtype.
